extraction_text: The speaker questions how they can understand the yoga being taught first by the listener, since the listener was born after Vivasvan.
Bhagavan explains that both he and Arjuna have undergone many births, but only Bhagavan remembers them all.
Bhagavan states that although his soul is unborn and imperishable, and he is the Lord of all beings, he still takes birth according to his own nature and through his own divine power (maya).
Bhagavan declares that he creates himself whenever righteousness (dharma) declines and unrighteousness (adharma) prevails, in order to protect the good, destroy the wicked, and re-establish dharma.
Bhagavan states that whoever truly understands his divine birth and actions, upon leaving the body, will not be born again but will attain him.
Bhagavan describes the qualities of those who attain him: free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in him, taking refuge in him, purified by the austerity of wisdom.
Bhagavan states that he accepts all who come to him, and that people everywhere follow his path.
Bhagavan explains that those desiring success in action worship the gods in this world, as action quickly yields results in the human realm.
Bhagavan declares that he created the four social orders (varnas) according to qualities and actions, yet he remains the unchanging creator.
Bhagavan explains that actions do not taint him, nor does he desire their fruits; one who understands this is not bound by action.
Bhagavan instructs Arjuna to act as the ancients who sought liberation did, having learned about them.
Bhagavan promises to explain the nature of action, inaction, and wrong action, which even the wise find confusing, so that Arjuna may be freed from evil.
Bhagavan describes the wise person who sees inaction in action and action in inaction as a yogi who accomplishes all actions.
Bhagavan explains that one whose actions are burned in the fire of wisdom, who acts without desire or selfish motive, is considered wise.
Bhagavan describes the person who acts without attachment to results, is content with what comes by chance, free from duality and envy, and equipoised in success and failure as unbound.
Bhagavan states that one whose intellect is established in wisdom, who has abandoned attachment and is free from bondage, who acts for sacrifice alone, sees their action completely dissolved.
Bhagavan explains that Brahman is the sacrifice, the offering, and the fire into which the offering is poured; one who contemplates action as Brahman attains Brahman.
Bhagavan describes different types of yogis: some offer sacrifices to the gods, others offer sacrifices into the fire of Brahman.
Bhagavan explains that some offer the senses (like hearing) into the fire of restraint, while others offer sense objects (like sound) into the fire of the senses.
Bhagavan states that others offer all activities of the life force and senses into the yoga-fire of self-control kindled by wisdom.
Arjuna asks Krishna to clarify which is better between renunciation of action and yoga of action.
Krishna explains that both renunciation of action and yoga of action lead to supreme bliss, but yoga of action is better than renunciation of action.

attributes.supernatural_element: Divine wisdom from Krishna (avatar of Vishnu)

extraction_text: Krishna describes the true renouncer as one without hatred or desire, free from dualities, who easily attains liberation.
Krishna explains that fools see Sankhya (knowledge) and Yoga (action) as different, while the wise see them as one, and following either correctly yields both fruits.
Krishna states that without Yoga, renunciation is difficult to reach Brahman, but with Yoga, the sage quickly attains Brahman.
Krishna concludes that through Yoga, one purifies oneself, controls the self, masters the senses, identifies with the Self of all beings, and remains unpolluted even while acting.
